about: The workflow crosswalk: every decision point of the AI-native SDLC playbook (the article, print pages of docs/reference/ai-native-sdlc-playbook.pdf) set against the sdlc framework (plugin 0.2.27, commit cf3f696); the row setup-adopt was added on 2026-09-30 against plugin 0.2.28, commit dd308ca. See ../2026-09-28-playbook-vs-framework.md. Re-checked on 2026-10-02 against plugin 0.2.29, commit 904f4ec: seven rows corrected for precision (setup-home, setup-gates, setup-merge, plan-idea, plan-ticket, plan-accept, x-roles); 0.2.28 and 0.2.29 change none of the others.

fields.stage: Setup, Plan, Design, Build, Test, Deploy, Maintain or Across stages
fields.why: Dn = decision n in docs/DECISIONS.md; "No decision" / "No Dn" = no decision behind the difference
fields.map: per side, [lane, kind, label]: lane P person, C Claude, A pipeline; kind d decision every change needs (Setup: once per project), c decision only in some cases, w work, r same act as another row
fields.target: optional: the owner's tentative proposal for this step, condensed from target-design.md; refs name its entries (T1, T2, ...)
fields.decision: optional: the owner's saved choice, copied from the crosswalk page's store at the end of a session (better: playbook | framework | both | neither | empty; decision: keep | adopt | blend | change | later; note; saved date; status: tentative until the whole study is done); the page's store stays the live copy

relations.same: both do it the same way
relations.added: the framework does something the article does not ask for
relations.missing: the article has it, the framework does not

rows.step: How much of the loop a project starts with, and in what order it grows
rows.pb: Adopt the plays in the order the dependency graph gives, which is not the stage order: start with any clay play (nothing points into it), and adopt any other play only after the plays whose arrows point into it. At first every step is prompted by hand; the end state is a loop in which each accepted artifact fires the next gate. For the design pass the ladder is by hand, then an organization slash command, then a job that fires on the merge. In Build, auto-accept becomes the default for routine work only as the guardrails from the later plays mature. The steps are modular, and organizations may choose to transform different stages at different times, based on their needs.
rows.fw: /sdlc:sdlc-init installs the whole loop in one change-0000 PR: every phase command, hook and gate, the twelve sdlc-*.yml workflows and phase (f)'s detection and scans. The loop runs in CI once the owner adds the Claude secret and lets GitHub Actions open pull requests (sdlc-init §6); until the secret exists every phase run ends green as 'skipped' (the weekly scan fails instead) and each phase is run by hand as a slash command, all phases alike. No setting starts a project with a subset of the plays or adds them in order: the profile sets how many gates wait for the owner, the review mode whether a judgment item parks or goes to the panel, deploy.production only whether a release label is needed, and sdlc.yaml's paused flag stops every phase run at once, not a chosen few. The evals suite starts empty and fills from incidents (D17), and the detection has nothing to watch until the project has CI runs of its own; neither is an adoption step the owner orders. The p.8 order and the p.13 ladder were used to build the framework itself (build guide stages B0 to B5, step 43), not to adopt it in a project.
rows.fwSrc: plugin/commands/sdlc-init.md §3 and §6, plugin/init/sdlc_init.py WORKFLOW_FILES, template/.github/workflows/, plugin/ci/auth.py, plugin/ci/run_phase.py (guard), template/sdlc.yaml paused, docs/BUILD_GUIDE.md step 43
rows.why: No decision on how a project adopts the framework. Nearest: D1 hosted CI (the p.13 ladder was applied to building the framework: by hand in B1, CI from B3) · D19 phase adapters, so no project skips (e) or (f) · D17 evals start empty
rows.weigh: The article adopts the plays in the p.8 order and runs each step by hand before automating it (p.8, p.13); the framework starts a project at the end state. It has no staged start: the nearest is to hold back the Claude secret, which leaves every phase to be run by hand, all at once. For a new project, is the full loop from the first change what you want, or should the framework offer a staged start?

pb: Organization picks which stages to transform first
Adopt the plays in the p.8 order

fw: Then each merge fires the next phase

decision.note: Blend: the whole loop from the first change stays the default (keep: no staged adoption, no per-phase switches). Added, nothing replaced: (#2) an optional, documented by-hand start - leave the Claude secret out, each phase job ends 'skipped' and I run the phase commands myself (the weekly scan fails until then); adding the secret later turns the automation on, nothing else changes (sdlc-init §6, README). (#3) the change-0000 intent lists what starts empty: evals (D17), lessons, CLAUDE.md 'Things Claude gets wrong', and the detection, which needs a CI workflow of the project's own and about 16 days of daily CI data before its first verdict (sdlc_init.py). Counting call: the playbook's adoption choice is a Setup decision (14 + 2).

rows.step: Where intents live and who sets it up
rows.pb: A one-time task for the platform or engineering team: a technical team member stands up the intent home and decides who can write to it. For a single product the simplest home is an intent/ folder in the product repo; a dedicated intent repo is only worth it when intent spans many repositories. The template, which can be encoded as a skill, is set up by a technical team member and signed off by a lead.
rows.fw: /sdlc:sdlc-init writes the project's files into the repository in one change-0000 PR: sdlc.yaml, guardrails, changes/, bands.yaml, evals/, lessons/, workflows. Intents live in changes/<id>-<slug>/ next to the code. Who can write to main is the branch ruleset of D4, which the owner creates by hand after the merge. The intent template is the intent-template skill, which ships in the plugin, so by default a project has no template to set up or sign off.
rows.why: D8 plugin + template · D9 the repo is the source of truth · D10 changes/<id>-<slug>/ · D4 the ruleset decides who writes to main
rows.weigh: p.10 calls an intent/ folder in the product repo the simplest home for a single product, which is where changes/ already sits; a dedicated intent repo only pays off when intent spans many repositories. D10 says that is not your case; does that still hold?

pb: Technical team member stands up the intent home
A lead signs off the template skill

target.text: Ideas stay in changes/<id>-<slug>/, set up by /sdlc-init. Intents can be written from Claude Code or from claude.ai / phone; you accept by merging, after the role briefs (T1). The intent template: the plugin default, overridable per project (to verify), reviewed by a Product role and approved by you. The intent gets an Examples/References section.

decision.note: Blend: ideas stay in changes/<id>-<slug>/, set up by /sdlc-init (current). I write intents from Claude Code or from claude.ai / phone. I accept by merging, after a Product role's brief (T1). Template: the plugin default, overridable per project (to verify); a Product role reviews it and I approve (T1). The intent gets an Examples/References section (T2).

rows.step: Which human approval gates exist, and where they are enforced
rows.pb: Engineering leadership, with change management and compliance, lists the gates that must survive; the platform engineer expresses each as a hook, with non-negotiable hooks in managed settings.
rows.fw: The gates are fixed by the framework (profiles, labels, confidence gate); per project, sdlc.yaml adds the risk list, protected paths and, on a declared production, the release approval and guarded deploy commands. /sdlc-init asks for the profile, the review mode and whether production is real; the risk list is the template's default, which it does not ask about. Guardrails sit in three layers: the plugin's hooks with project deny rules as a second net; an optional managed settings file, on the owner's machine only, which neither a cloud session nor CI reads; CI loading hooks and permissions from the pinned plugin, never from the PR branch. The owner adds the 'Restrict updates' ruleset.
rows.fwSrc: plugin/hooks/, template/.claude/settings.json, template/sdlc.yaml risk_list, plugin/commands/sdlc-init.md §1 and §6, docs/owner-machine/README.md
rows.why: D6 all three guardrail layers (the managed settings layer documented, not installed) · D18 profiles · D21 review mode · one owner, so no separate leadership list
rows.weigh: sdlc.yaml already lists the project's risk items, protected paths and guarded deploy commands. Is that your 'gates that must survive' list, or does each item need a named approver?

pb: Leadership lists the gates that must survive
Platform engineer writes each as a hook
fw: Owner picks profile, review mode, production

target.text: No new gates: (a), (b), (e) and (f) stay, with (c) and (d) in Full; sdlc.yaml's risk list, protected paths and production settings and today's enforcement stay (D6, D18 unchanged). At each gate you approve after the role briefs that gate names; a risk-list hit still parks, and the matching role's brief comes before your sdlc:accept-risk; your own edits to the gates themselves get a role's brief before you merge.

decision.note: Blend: gates stay as today, fixed (a), (b), (e), (f), with (c) and (d) in Full; no new gates. Project items stay in sdlc.yaml (risk list, protected paths, production settings); enforcement stays as today (plugin hooks, CI's pinned settings, optional managed settings, my ruleset). At each gate I approve after the role briefs that gate names (T1 approvals table). A risk-list hit parks; the matching role's brief, then my sdlc:accept-risk. My own edits to the gates themselves get a role's brief before I merge.

rows.pb: Not named. Intent acceptance 'is recorded as the merge'; code PRs need a code owner's approval through branch protection; the agent has no route to push to main.
rows.fw: Only the owner merges, once the owner has created a 'Restrict updates' ruleset on the default branch with the owner as the only bypass actor. The owner creates it by hand after the 0000 merge; the framework never creates it, and the daily digest warns while it is missing. Until it exists nothing stops the automation identity from pushing to or merging into the default branch; once it does, that identity has branch-only write access. sdlc-init §6 has the owner set the bypass mode to Exempt, so the rules, 'Require a pull request' included, do not run for the owner.
rows.why: D4 merge-restricted ruleset · D5 workflow token as the automation identity
rows.weigh: The article asks for branch protection with a code owner's approval and no agent route to main (p.33, p.40). D4 swaps the required approval for a merge restriction, because GitHub does not count the author's own approval. Who presses merge is gap 1 on the playbook page. Add a required review only if a second reviewer appears.

pb: Branch protection requires a code owner
fw: Ruleset: owner is the only bypass actor

target.text: You stay the only approver. The manager prepares a merge; you approve it from your account (a label or an approving review); a deterministic workflow, not a model, checks who approved and carries the merge out. sdlc-runbook.yml works this way today for the sdlc:go label, though it checks only that a person applied it, not that it was you. Would reopen or amend D4, D5, D13, D24. To verify: whether a ruleset lets a workflow merge for you, or a GitHub App is needed.

decision.note: Blend: I approve; the manager prepares the merge; a workflow merges after checking it was me (T1). No agent route to main, as today. No required review: role briefs (Code reviewer, Platform & release) before my approval, advice not enforced. The approval signal comes from my account and is checked as me, not just 'a person' (today's sdlc:go gap). Record: merge commit + my approval signal + the manager's recommendation in evidence/. Setup as today, plus (to verify) a ruleset setting or GitHub App that lets the workflow merge. Would reopen or amend D4, D5, D13, D24.

decision.note: Blend, added and nothing replaced: /sdlc-plan in Claude Code stays; a second route writes the intent from claude.ai on a computer or phone (T3), arriving as a PR on its branch, never a commit to main; the interview is fed by the roles and led by the manager (T1, T2). Correction and commit stay as today (they match the article). Open (T3): how a claude.ai intent gets its change id.

rows.step: A ticket or an alert becomes intent.md
rows.pb: An agent writes intent.md off the back of a ticket or an alert; the product owner reviews and corrects it before it is committed.
rows.fw: Alerts: the detect workflow runs /sdlc-maintain, which writes the incident intent; the scan workflow writes, without a diagnosis run, an intent for each Important finding it routes (at most max_findings, default 3, per run); each opens an incident PR. Tickets: no workflow triggers on an issue; the owner starts /sdlc:sdlc-plan with route 'ticket' and an external reference.
rows.why: Alerts: D15 (CI failure rate) and D16 (weekly security review). Tickets: no decision. D9 keeps the repo as the record, with tracker links; it does not rule out a ticket trigger.
rows.weigh: Is an automatic 'issue labelled X → intent PR' trigger worth adding, or do tickets stay manual?

PO reviews and corrects before commit

rows.pb: The product owner approves: acceptance is recorded as the merge, rejection as the closing review.
rows.fw: Gate (a): the owner merges the intent PR. Closing it without a merge abandons the change (sdlc-abandon.yml): every closed change gets status.yaml abandoned_reason 'pull request N closed without a merge' on its branches. An incident closed at its triage (gate (f)) also records a reason: the last comment by a repository member becomes the dismissal reason, in a dismissal PR the owner merges; with no such comment nothing is dismissed.
rows.why: D25 close = abandon
rows.weigh: Nothing to decide unless you want a recorded rejection reason for ideas and tickets too; incidents record one when you comment before closing.

rows.step: Who writes the policy skills, and whether a project adds its own
rows.pb: An engineer writes each skill from the policy owner's written source of truth, tests that it triggers by asking for the task in different ways, and the policy owner signs off changes. Skills sit in the repo's .claude/skills/ or ship organization-wide in a plugin; engineers pick up a new version automatically in their next session.
rows.fw: Five generic policy skills ship in the plugin, written by the framework from the article; each says 'no owner source yet'. A project may add .claude/skills/<name>/, which the design command (not the build command) treats as replacing the plugin's, and spec.md's header records the override; .claude/** is a guardrail path, so only the owner adds one. The phase jobs pick up a new skill version only when the owner bumps the plugin pin in sdlc.yaml, and no eval checks that a policy skill triggers.
rows.why: D8 plugin + pinned version · D6 .claude/** is the owner's · build guide step 20 (generic skills, project override). Owner sources and trigger testing: no decision.
rows.weigh: The skills have no named source. Is there a written policy of yours (security, data) a skill should be derived from, and should each skill get one eval that asks for the task without naming the skill (p.22 step 4)?

pb: Engineer writes and trigger-tests each skill
fw: Generic skills ship in the plugin

rows.pb: Hooks can block edits to migrations and infra without an approved change ticket; the gate defines what counts as approval (an approved change ticket or the release manager's sign-off). A hook can also ask, pausing until a specific person approves, which release gating uses.
rows.fw: The risk list in sdlc.yaml (auth, data migrations, money movement, production config): a hit parks the change at its next gate; the owner accepts with sdlc:accept-risk. No mid-run 'ask'.

rows.weigh: Park-at-the-gate replaces ask-mid-run. A risk item the design foresees is a flagged concern and parks at gate (b), before any code is written; one the design missed is found in the diff at the next gate, after the work.

Skill and hook changes ship in the plugin and are tested by the framework's own suite (framework-evals.yml); a project's pin bump does not trigger its sdlc-evals.yml.

rows.fw: The REVIEW.md pass runs once per change, at (e), in a fresh-context CI job; a fix loop runs while an Important finding stands. The intent and spec PRs get no REVIEW.md pass.

rows.pb: When Claude makes a mistake twice, the correction goes into CLAUDE.md. Review puts it there as part of the review that flags it the second time, and also flags when a change has made CLAUDE.md outdated. Code owners approve the edit in PR review.
rows.fw: The (e) review records each finding's signature in changes/.review-seen.json. A finding seen again in a later change, or one about CLAUDE.md itself, becomes a proposed 'Things Claude gets wrong' line in evidence/claude-md-proposals.md, quoted in the PR description. The run cannot edit CLAUDE.md; the owner applies the line in a commit of their own.

rows.weigh: A repeat is matched on an exact signature (pass, file, normalised summary), so a reworded repeat is missed, and only review findings count, not mistakes seen in a session. Should the daily digest list proposals you have not applied yet?

fw: Owner applies it in a commit of their own

rows.pb: Once a month the tech lead tunes the setup by rating findings so the reviewer improves and by capping Nit volume in REVIEW.md; generated paths and anything CI already enforces are excluded.
rows.fw: REVIEW.md ships with the nit cap (at most five, the rest as a count) and a 'Do not report' list, and the tally keeps the reviewer's count of omitted nits. Nothing rates findings and no periodic tuning runs; REVIEW.md changes only by the owner's hand.
rows.why: No Dn: build guide sub-step 26.5 (monthly tuning), recorded 'not built' (ROADMAP Milestone 1 item 1)
rows.weigh: Without ratings, the only tuning signal is what you notice at gate (e). The build guide planned 'a scheduled agent PR you merge or ignore' (step 26), but a run cannot edit REVIEW.md (D6), so such a job would have to propose the edit as text, like claude-md-proposals.md. Worth adding, or is tuning by hand enough for one owner?

rows.pb: A reviewer or the author tags @claude on a review comment; Claude addresses it and pushes. For PRs Claude opened, a slash command babysits until green.
rows.fw: The owner's 'Request changes' review (or an un-park label) runs sdlc-fix.yml: comments become constraints, the phase re-runs, iterations + 1. No @claude trigger.
rows.why: D22 'Request changes' starts the fix run · D24 un-park labels
rows.weigh: One comment at a time (@claude) vs one review round at a time. The framework's is coarser but cheaper to run.

rows.pb: A code owner approves through branch protection, informed by the findings; the agent that wrote the code cannot approve it. The stage table reserves human review for regulated and critical code.
rows.fw: Gate (e): the owner merges the build PR, which stays a draft until sdlc:e-ready. The draft is the only guard against an early merge.
rows.why: D4 · D13 gate (e) is the merge
rows.weigh: See issue #66: an early merge releases unreviewed code and later releases again.

fw: Gate (e): owner merges the build PR

target.text: Code reviewer (today's REVIEW.md pass) and Platform & release briefs; the manager recommends merge or request changes; you approve, and the merge runs on your signal.

rows.pb: Start with read-only judgment steps: claude -p in a pipeline job to triage a failed build, summarize a flaky test or draft the changelog; then write steps.
rows.fw: Read-only claude -p judgment jobs exist in CI: the REVIEW.md pass, the weekly security review, and the 2σ/3σ diagnosis, which reads failed runs with gh run view. The article's three example jobs (failed-build triage, flaky-test summary, changelog draft) are missing; release notes come from release/notes.py, deterministically (no model), after gate (e).
rows.why: No decision on the three example jobs
rows.weigh: A 'triage failed build' job is cheap and read-only. Worth adding?

rows.pb: Development: the agent deploys freely; staging in the middle; production: the agent prepares the release. Deploy, status and rollback exposed as MCP tools per environment.
rows.fw: One deploy adapter per project (deploy.action: publish package, schedule job, regenerate report, promote to paper trading, deploy service, none) running deploy.command; deploy.production true/false is the one tier switch. Deploy, status and rollback as MCP tools are decided but not built until an adapter names a real deployment.
rows.why: D13 the merge is the whole gate until a real production · D19 phase adapters · build guide step 31 (tools deferred)
rows.weigh: Do any of your projects need a dev/staging tier before production?

pb: Agent deploys dev; prepares prod release

rows.pb: The production deploy hook blocks the release until a named release manager authorizes it; the agent cannot pass the gate.
rows.fw: With deploy.production: true the owner applies sdlc:release-approved: the release workflow waits for the label (release/cli.py checks it; no Claude session runs there), and the production_gate hook blocks guarded deploy commands in any Claude session until then; it blocks, never asks. Without it the merge alone releases.
rows.why: D13 option 1
rows.weigh: See issue #68: a parked build PR merged at (e) releases without its park reason shown again.

target.text: On a declared production, a Platform & release brief (the release checklist) before your release approval.

rows.pb: The service owner or platform engineer picks one metric; a deterministic script (Western Electric or similar) flags breaches; tiers in bands.yaml: 1σ logs, 2σ read-only diagnosis, 3σ acts through gated routes.
rows.fw: sdlc-detect.yml, daily: CI test failure rate against bands.yaml, Western Electric rules, no model; 1σ logs, 2σ and 3σ file an incident.
rows.why: D15 CI test failure rate first
rows.weigh: Close match. A production metric is the next step (D15).

fw: Daily detect on CI failure rate

rows.pb: Claude is invoked read-only to diagnose and writes its diagnosis as intent.md in the Stage 1 format.
rows.fw: /sdlc:sdlc-maintain --diagnosis-only reads lessons/, investigates read-only and writes the incident intent.md and proposal.json; the detect job's finish step opens the incident PR.
rows.weigh: Close match.

fw: Finish step opens the incident PR

rows.pb: The service owner or on-call engineer triages the queue: fix now, schedule, dismiss; product-facing findings go to the product owner. Dismissals tune the bands.
rows.fw: Gate (f): the owner triages the incident PR. Merge = fix now (it is gate (a) of the incident change); 'schedule' label = later; close with a member's comment = a dismissal PR to merge, which suppresses the finding's signature (a detection for one baseline window, a scan finding for good); tuning the bands is a separate bands.yaml PR.
rows.why: D25 per-finding triage
rows.weigh: The dismissal needs a second merge. Is that friction worth the audit trail?

pb: Service owner triages: fix, schedule, dismiss
fw: Gate (f): owner triages the incident PR

target.text: Operations brief (Security & policy for scans); the manager recommends fix now, schedule or dismiss; you triage.

rows.pb: Claude may act only by opening a PR into the review gate or triggering a pre-approved runbook. The Claude Tag example still asks 'shall I run it?' and waits for 'Go.'.
rows.fw: Split by blast radius: quarantine-flaky-test and revert-pr are pre-approved and run unattended, each opening its own PR; rollback-deploy waits for the owner's sdlc:go; a rehearsed rollback on a declared production is pre-approved.
rows.why: D14 split by blast radius · D26 rehearsed rollback pre-approved
rows.weigh: D26 goes one step past the article (no 'Go' for a rehearsed rollback). Still comfortable with that?

fw: Owner merges or closes each runbook PR

rows.pb: When the fix ships, add an eval for the incident; the post-mortem goes to a version-controlled lessons file.
rows.fw: An incident change's (e) run is told to write lessons/<yyyy-mm>-<slug>.md and one eval case; the next diagnosis reads lessons/. No gate checks them; not yet exercised live.
rows.weigh: Make the lesson and the eval case a gate check at (e) for incident changes?

rows.pb: Claude Security on a schedule (weekly is a sensible default); each finding validated with a confidence rating; dismissed with a reason; suggested patch reviewed in Claude Code on the web; eval for the vulnerability class.
rows.fw: sdlc-scan.yml, weekly: a security review plus deterministic scanners; up to 3 Important findings per run filed as incident PRs from a template intent, without a diagnosis run.
rows.why: D16 the pattern without Claude Security
rows.weigh: No confidence rating and no diagnosis for scan findings. Is the finding quality good enough?

fw: Owner triages each scan PR at gate (f)

target.text: A Security & policy brief on each scan finding; the manager recommends fix now, schedule or dismiss; you triage.

rows.step: Claude on call in a channel
rows.pb: Claude is a member of the incident channel under its own identity; anyone there can guide and action the response; a person says 'Go.'; the channel is the audit trail.
rows.fw: No chat channel. The nearest equivalents are the incident PR, the sdlc:go label and lessons/.
rows.why: No Dn: build guide step 40 records a chat entry route as optional and unbuilt (ROADMAP, Milestone 1 item 1). D20 rules out notifications to the owner, not a chat entry route.
rows.weigh: Real-time response vs no notifications. Only matters once a project runs live.

rows.pb: An independent confidence gate between stages, a deterministic check or an adversarial reviewing agent, decides whether the output continues or is escalated to a human. The article does not say which check, the thresholds or which human.
rows.fw: Run limits, then deterministic checks, then the adversarial verdict (b-d) or the REVIEW.md pass (e); outcomes continue, wait (ready label) or park (sdlc:needs-human, 'What I need from you').
rows.why: D11 park, never page · D18 · D21
rows.weigh: The framework makes concrete what the article leaves open (gap 6 on the playbook page).

fw: Owner at a ready or parked PR

rows.step: How finished work reaches a person
rows.pb: Human attention concentrates at the gates, reviewing what the agent flagged. The article names a triage queue for maintain findings (p.44-45) and counts failures 'triaged without paging a human' (p.41), but describes no review queue or digest for finished work.
rows.fw: Nothing notifies the owner: ready and parked PRs wait in the PR list, summarised daily in one 'SDLC review queue' issue; every PR opens with a short bulleted summary.
rows.why: D11 · D20 queue + digest
rows.weigh: Is one daily digest enough, or do some parks deserve a ping?

rows.step: Sandbox, tokens and identity of agent jobs
rows.pb: Agent jobs run in containers under a network policy with short-lived scoped tokens and no standing production credentials. Each non-interactive run acts under the agent's own identity, so the log separates what the agent did from what the person who triggered it did.
rows.fw: Every phase job runs claude -p on an ephemeral GitHub runner with settings from the pinned framework: the sandbox is mandatory, the network is limited to the API, GitHub and package registries, secrets and web tools are denied and bypass is disabled. The session gets one model credential (the runner drops the other) and the workflow token, and it commits as github-actions[bot]. No phase job holds a deploy secret; the release job runs deploy.command with no Claude session.
rows.why: D1 hosted CI · D5 workflow token as the agent's identity · D6 layer iii (settings from the pinned plugin)
rows.weigh: The session keeps GITHUB_TOKEN (in the (b)-(e) and fix jobs: contents, pull requests, issues, checks and actions write) because it pushes and labels; the article's example strips it from sandboxed commands (p.37). Is that acceptable while the token has no route to main (D4)?

rows.pb: None for runs. The article bounds what the agent may do, not how long or how much it may try; it mentions money only as 'an API key with budget for eval runs' and a spend limit set centrally for Claude Security scans.
rows.fw: Each unattended run is bounded by 3 fix iterations per change (2 when non-routine), 4 panel calls per change under deferred review, 120 minutes per phase run, --max-turns 200 per session, an optional dollar cap (max_budget_usd, off by default) and a paused flag read from the default branch. An iteration, panel, clock or budget limit parks the change with its partial evidence; a pause skips every run before it starts. The owner lifts an iteration-cap park with the sdlc:reset-iterations label.
rows.why: D11 a limit hit parks · build guide step 19 (tagged ADDED; D1 relies on it to bound API cost)
rows.weigh: With the dollar cap off, only turns, iterations, panel calls and the clock bound spend. When set, the cap is compared with the last session's cost in the phase (record-spend overwrites the figure), not a sum per change as sdlc.yaml and D1 say. Set a cap, and should it be summed per change?

rows.pb: Every play ends with 'How to measure it': a leading and a lagging indicator, read from records that already exist (git history, PR metadata, CI logs, the OpenTelemetry export, the incident tracker), such as time to first review, first-pass CI success rate, time waiting at each gate and DORA measures.
rows.fw: Each PR description carries two counters: first-pass merge and fix iterations (plus panel calls when there are any). The daily digest adds a Counters table (first-pass merge share, fix iterations per shipped change, panel calls, incidents merged and shipped, dismissals), computed with no model. The eval report gives a pass rate, and detection.json has the breach time and tier; nothing else is computed.
rows.why: No decision on which indicators to compute: build guide step 42 (two counters now, a scheduled report later). D20 sets only the channel (the digest, pull not push), not what is measured.
rows.weigh: Spend is recorded per run but summed nowhere, and time waiting at your gates is not counted. Which one or two indicators would change a decision of yours?

rows.pb: Evidence is logged in the session transcript, forwarded by OpenTelemetry, and in the PR's check run. Hook allow/block decisions and maintain invocations, findings and triage decisions are logged with a timestamp; the chain of commits is the audit trail.
rows.fw: Each change keeps its record in git: evidence/ holds each claude -p run's JSON result (final message, turns, cost and permission denials, not the full conversation), run and gate records, verdicts, findings and the panel ledger; gate (d) and the review pass also post check runs. Every hook decision is a timestamped line in evidence/hook-log.jsonl, also uploaded as a workflow artifact, while status.yaml names who applied each un-park label and sdlc:go, and .dismissed.json who dismissed what, and when. No OpenTelemetry export.
rows.fwSrc: plugin/hooks/_common.py log_decision, plugin/ci/run_phase.py, plugin/gate/artifacts.py, plugin/state/status.py, plugin/detect/dismissals.py, plugin/pr/cli.py check-run
rows.why: D9 the repo is the record (evidence in git). OpenTelemetry export: no decision; build guide step 41 defers it ('only if you later want dashboards').
rows.weigh: An unattended run leaves its result and its hook log but not its full transcript. Is that enough to reconstruct what a parked run did, or should runs keep the transcript?

target.text: Role briefs (evidence/roles/) and the manager's recommendation (evidence/manager.md) are committed with the change; full transcripts are kept as workflow artifacts until they expire (GitHub's default is 90 days).

rows.pb: Distinct roles: originator, product owner, policy owners, engineer, tech lead or architect, code owner, platform engineer, release manager, service owner or on-call, security lead.
rows.fw: One owner holds the seven roles OPERATING_MODEL.md §2 names (originator, product owner, tech lead, engineer, code owner, release manager, service owner). The policy owners, the platform engineer and the security lead are not named there, and no policy owner's source exists yet: the five policy skills are written from the article and say 'no owner source yet'. Separation of duties is rebuilt from three things: writer ≠ judge (a different agent in a fresh context reviews, and only the owner approves), an automation identity distinct from the owner's account, and branch rules that keep merges to the owner (once the owner has created the ruleset).
rows.why: The framework's premise: one owner, hands-off
rows.weigh: The one structural question behind many rows. Where does collapsing roles lose a check you want?

fw: One owner holds the seven named roles

target.text: Six AI roles in a first cut to adjust (Product, Architect, Code reviewer, Security & policy, Platform & release, Operations) write briefs from their own sources; one manager reads them all and recommends; you stay the only approver. Open: which models, which sources, how many roles.

targets.status: tentative until the whole study is done

The intent home: in the repository, written from anywhere, with examples
